unlock.subUnlock: Enter your master password. Without it nobody reaches your saved connections.
unlock.subCreate: Choose a master password. It encrypts every stored password and key (AES-256-GCM). Once the vault exists you will get a recovery key in case you ever forget it.
unlock.subRecovery: Enter your recovery key and pick a new master password. The old one stops working.
unlock.noRecovery: This vault has no recovery key — a forgotten password cannot be recovered.
recovery.title: Recovery key
recovery.introNew: Your vault is ready. This key gets you back to your data if you ever forget the master password.
recovery.introRegenerated: The new recovery key is active. The previous one stopped working just now.
recovery.warningBody: We store the key nowhere — the vault holds a lock derived from it, not the key itself. Anyone who has it reaches every stored password and private key, so keep it separate from the vault file.
recovery.confirm: I have stored the key somewhere safe
recovery.fileBody1: This key resets a forgotten master password and grants access to every stored connection, password and key.
recovery.fileBody2: Keep it separate from the vault file — for example in a password manager or on paper.
conn.name: Name
conn.keyStoredPlaceholder: (stored — paste a new key only if you want to replace it)
conn.ppkError: This is a PuTTY-format key (.ppk). Convert it in PuTTYgen via “Conversions → Export OpenSSH key”.
conn.keyRequired: To sign in with a key you have to paste one or load it from a file.
conn.deleteBody: Really delete {{name}} ({{user}}@{{host}})? The stored password and key will be gone for good.
snip.empty: No saved commands or notes yet.
snip.title: Name
snip.notePlaceholder: What it is for, what to watch out for…
snip.insertTitle: Inserts the text into the terminal; you press Enter yourself
snip.runTitle: Inserts the text and sends it
snip.multiline: Multiple lines — in a shell every line ending acts as Enter.
snip.multilineWarn: The command has multiple lines. In a terminal every line ending acts as Enter, so all of them will run one after another.
snip.noSession: Open the session you want the command inserted into first.
snip.confirmBody: {{title}} has multiple lines. Every line ending acts as Enter in a shell, so all of them will run on {{session}}, one after another.
snip.deleteBody: Really delete {{title}}? The content will be gone for good.
term.noSessionHint: Pick a connection on the left and click it.
term.runHeader: AI command — runs in its own channel, not in this shell:
term.runTimedOut: AI command hit the time limit and may still be running.
hostkey.bodyUnknown: You are connecting to {{host}}:{{port}} for the first time. Verify the key fingerprint — for example with ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub on the server itself — and only then accept it.
hostkey.bodyChanged: The key fingerprint of {{host}}:{{port}} does not match the one you have stored. It may be a legitimate change, such as a reinstalled server, but it may also be an attempt to intercept the connection. Continue only if you expect the change and have verified the new fingerprint through another channel.
settings.title: Settings
settings.languageHint: Missing or wrong translation? Contributions are welcome.
settings.disconnectOnLock: End all SSH sessions when locking
settings.recoveryHint: A fallback way to reach your data when you forget the master password. It is stored nowhere — the vault holds only a lock derived from it.
settings.recoveryWarn: Generating a new key invalidates the old one immediately. Removing it costs you the only rescue for a forgotten password.
settings.recoveryConfirmHint: Enter your master password. This re-encrypts the vault under a new key, which is what makes the old recovery key genuinely stop working.
settings.changePasswordHint: Re-wraps the vault key with a new password. The old one stops working immediately.
settings.passwordMismatch: The new passwords do not match.
link.confirmBody: This link came from the application or from terminal output. Check the full address before opening it.
settings.mcpIntro: Exposes your sessions to an AI client such as Claude Code through a local MCP server on 127.0.0.1. Server addresses, usernames and passwords are never sent — the AI sees only session names. You approve every command and every read of the output.
settings.mcpWarn: the commands the AI proposes and the output you release. Your AI client sends them to its provider. Credentials stay here, output does not.
settings.mcpTokenPlaceholder: generated when you turn it on
settings.mcpRegenerated: The token was regenerated — set it again in your AI client.
settings.mcpTokenCopied: The token is now in the clipboard, where any program on this machine can read it. Paste it into your AI client, and regenerate it if it ended up anywhere else.
settings.mcpTokenHint: The token grants access to your sessions — treat it like a password. It does not expire; regenerating it is how you revoke it, and you then have to set it again in the AI client. Copying puts it on the system clipboard, which every program can read and which Windows keeps in its clipboard history — ConsoleWard cannot clear that.
mcp.multilineWarn: The command contains several lines — all of them will run one after another.
mcp.commandClippedWarn: The command is taller than the box — scroll to the end of it before you approve.
mcp.injectionWarn: The proposal was built from text that may have come out of the server's own output. Read it even when it looks harmless.
mcp.separateShellWarn: This will NOT run in your open terminal. It gets its own channel on the same connection: a fresh shell in the home directory, without your aliases, shell functions or PATH additions, and with no way to answer a password prompt.
mcp.autoShare: Send the output automatically once it finishes — unless it looks like it contains a credential
mcp.autoShareOverridden: This output was going to be sent automatically. It looks like it contains a credential, so you are being shown it first. Nothing has been sent yet.
mcp.shareTitleRead: The AI is asking for terminal output
mcp.detectedTail: The highlighting is only a hint — read the rest as well.
mcp.detectedIncomplete: Only the first {{limit}} of each kind are highlighted — the text holds more.
mcp.scanClipped: Only the first {{kb}} KB were checked. Nothing below that point is highlighted, whatever it holds — read it yourself before you send it.
mcp.chooseHint: Nothing has been sent yet. Choose what the AI gets to see — you will be shown it again before it leaves.
mcp.pickUnavailable: This session no longer has an open console, so you can only send the last lines it produced.
mcp.pickHint: Drag across the terminal to highlight what should be sent.
mcp.pickLost: The console for this session has closed. Nothing can be selected from it now.
mcp.shareHint: Exactly what is here will be sent — you can edit or delete anything. The AI is told that it is an excerpt.
secret.assignment: password or key in an assignment
error.vaultMissing: The vault does not exist yet.
error.wrongOldPassword: The old password does not match.
error.passwordTooShort: The master password must be at least {{length}} characters long.
password.weak: Weak — easy to guess offline. Longer helps more than punctuation does.
password.fair: Fair — it would hold up against a casual attempt.
password.hint: Four or five unrelated words beat any amount of punctuation. This is the one password that opens everything else, and it cannot be recovered — only reset with your recovery key.
error.decryptFailed: The vault content could not be decrypted — the file is damaged.
error.noPasswordSet: The vault has no master password set. Use the recovery key.
error.noRecoverySet: This vault has no recovery key.
error.recoveryLength: The recovery key must be {{length}} characters long ({{actual}} entered).
error.recoveryChar: The recovery key contains an invalid character “{{char}}”.
error.legacyNoRecovery: This vault was created in the old format and has no recovery key.
error.lastUnlockMethod: Cannot remove the only way to unlock the vault.
error.noUnlockMethod: The vault has no way to unlock it.
error.invalidPort: The port must be a whole number between 1 and 65535.
error.fileTooLarge: The file is too large — the limit is 1 MB.
error.notRegularFile: That is not an ordinary file — pick a key stored on disk.
error.unknownSetting: The settings contain an item this version does not know, so nothing was saved.
error.unexpected: Something went wrong. The details are in the application log.
error.commandRunning: A command is already running in this session.
error.authFailed: Authentication failed — wrong password, key or user.
error.mcpVaultLocked: The vault has to be unlocked.
error.mcpBridgeMissing: The MCP bridge is not connected.
error.portInUse: Port {{port}} is already used by another application.
error.serverStartFailed: The server could not be started: {{message}}
error.execFailed: The command could not be started in its own channel: {{message}}
error.invalidMcpPort: The port must be a whole number between 1024 and 65535.
vault.rollbackTitle: This vault is older than the one you last used.
vault.rollbackBody: The file on disk is at write {{found}}; the last one seen was {{expected}}, on {{date}}. Someone may have put an older copy back, or a backup was restored.
vault.rollbackHostKeys: Saved host fingerprints may be out of date, so a server whose key really did change can look like a first connection. Read any host-key prompt carefully until you have sorted this out.
